ZZ-Free bSWAP Gates under Strong Driving
in Far-Detuned Fixed-Frequency Transmons

Akinori Machino 1,2,∗    Kazuhisa Ogawa 2,3    Yuto Ikegai 2    Takafumi Miyanaga 2    Koichiro Ban 3    Nilton F. G. Filho 1,2    Hidehisa Shiomi 2    Toshi Sumida 4    Shuhei Tamate 5    Yutaka Tabuchi 5,2    Yasunobu Nakamura 5,6    Makoto Negoro 1,2,3,†
1Graduate School of Engineering Science, The University of Osaka, Toyonaka, Osaka, Japan
2Center for Quantum Information and Quantum Biology, The University of Osaka, Toyonaka, Osaka, Japan
3Graduate School of Information Science and Technology, The University of Osaka, Suita, Osaka, Japan

6Graduate School of Engineering, The University of Tokyo, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo, Japan
∗Contact author: akinori.machino@qiqb.osaka-u.ac.jp
†Contact author: negoro.makoto.qiqb@osaka-u.ac.jp
Abstract

Far-detuned frequency allocations in fixed-frequency superconducting processors mitigate spectral crowding but constrain cross-resonance interactions at practical drive amplitudes. Here, we demonstrate that a single strong drive induces a large XX−YYXX-YYXX−YY interaction in the far-detuned regime, while a weak second tone tunes the accompanying ZZZZZZ phase. The interaction realizes a 150150150-ns bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​ gate, which can directly prepare a maximally entangled state from the ground state. For the implementations on the same qubit pair at matched drive strengths, cross resonance gives a shorter CNOT operation, while bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​ gives a 33%33\%33% shorter SWAP operation with a higher IRB fidelity. The multilevel theory further predicts a regime where stronger driving can yield a speed advantage for CNOT as well, a possibility absent in the two-level model. As an application of the XX−YYXX-YYXX−YY interaction, we also demonstrate two-spin squeezing beyond the standard quantum limit through two-axis countertwisting. The interaction realized here complements cross resonance and offers a route to efficient gate synthesis and quantum simulation of interacting spin systems.

I. Introduction

Cross-resonance (CR) gates are widely used in fixed-frequency, fixed-coupling superconducting architectures, where driving one qubit at its neighbor’s transition frequency induces an effective ZXZXZX interaction used to implement CNOT operations [1, 2, 3, 4]. Far-detuned frequency allocations can mitigate spectral crowding [5, 6], but larger qubit-frequency separations reduce the CR interaction strength for a given coupling and drive amplitude [7, 8, 9]. Practical upper limits on drive amplitude therefore motivate additional native gates that complement CR for more efficient compilation of a broader range of quantum circuits.

In addition to CR, a range of entangling gates has been proposed and demonstrated in fixed-frequency superconducting architectures. These approaches include conditional-phase gates [10, 11, 12, 13, 14] and population-exchange gates [15, 16, 17, 18, 19]. The CZ gate realized through a conditional-phase interaction is locally equivalent to a CNOT operation, whereas iSWAP and bSWAP belong to a different local-equivalence class under the Cartan decomposition [20]. Native exchange gates therefore provide complementary building blocks for gate synthesis alongside CR [19, 21].

Stark iSWAP and bSWAP gates induce coherent population exchange within the odd- and even-parity subspaces, respectively. Both gates can be activated by microwave drives detuned from the individual qubit transitions [19]. Stark bSWAP is particularly attractive for far-detuned qubits because it can reach two-photon resonance without closing the large frequency gap. However, the fixed-frequency demonstration in Ref. 19 was performed in the straddling regime and used a two-level approximation for its analytical description. Whether Stark bSWAP gates could be realized under strong driving in far-detuned multilevel transmons remained untested.

Strong off-resonant driving of multilevel transmons can generate a substantial ZZZZZZ interaction alongside the desired bSWAP exchange. The resulting conditional phase must be compensated to realize an ideal bSWAP gate. Because the XX−YYXX-YYXX−YY and ZZZZZZ interactions commute, the ZZZZZZ phase can be controlled separately from the exchange. We exploit this property by combining the bSWAP drive with a second tone on the other qubit to tune ZZZZZZ through Stark-induced ZZZZZZ by level excursions (siZZle) [22, 23, 24]. This approach supports both ideal bSWAP gates and a tunable combination of XX−YYXX-YYXX−YY and ZZZZZZ interactions for quantum simulation [18].

In this work, we develop a multilevel dressed-state theory of these interactions and experimentally demonstrate bSWAP and bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​ gates in a far-detuned transmon pair. We characterize the gates using randomized and cross-entropy benchmarking. We compare the durations and fidelities of CNOT and SWAP implementations based on CR or bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​ on the same qubit pair at matched drive strengths, showing how these native gates complement each other. We also demonstrate two-spin squeezing beyond the standard quantum limit (SQL) using the XX−YYXX-YYXX−YY interaction.

The paper is organized as follows. Section II develops the multilevel theory of Stark bSWAP and ZZZZZZ control. Section III presents the experimental implementation, ZZZZZZ compensation, and gate benchmarking. Section IV discusses complementary native interactions and quantum-simulation applications, including two-spin squeezing. Section V summarizes the results. The appendices provide supporting theoretical derivations, experimental methods, and details of gate synthesis and comparison.

II. Stark bSWAP and ZZ control

We introduce the target bSWAP unitary and derive the XX−YYXX-YYXX−YY interaction and resonance condition in the dressed basis under a single drive. We then compare the two-level and multilevel models. An additional microwave tone controls the accompanying ZZZZZZ interaction.

II.3. ZZ control with siZZle

In multilevel transmon qubits, the XX−YYXX-YYXX−YY interaction in Sec. II.2 is accompanied by a ZZZZZZ interaction. Its coefficient ζ\zetaζ contains both the static ZZZZZZ coupling and the contribution induced by the drive on QA\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{A}}QA​. The interaction Hamiltonian can be written as

Hint=−JXY4(XX−YY)+ζ4ZZ.H_{\mathrm{int}}=-\frac{J_{XY}}{4}(XX-YY)+\frac{\zeta}{4}ZZ{}.Hint​=−4JXY​​(XX−YY)+4ζ​ZZ. (16)

The expression for ζ\zetaζ is derived in Appendix A.2.

Since the XX−YYXX-YYXX−YY and ZZZZZZ terms commute, their evolutions can be treated separately. We add a second tone on QB\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{B}}QB​ at the bSWAP drive frequency ωd\omega_{\mathrm{d}}ωd​ to control ζ\zetaζ through siZZle [23]. Its amplitude ΩB\Omega_{\mathrm{B}}ΩB​ and phase φ\varphiφ relative to the drive on QA\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{A}}QA​ serve as the control parameters for the ZZZZZZ interaction. With the drive on QA\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{A}}QA​ held fixed, a weak second tone changes the coefficient according to

ζ(ΩB,φ)≃ζ(0)+χZZΩBcos⁡φ,\zeta(\Omega_{\mathrm{B}},\varphi)\simeq\zeta(0)+\chi_{ZZ}\Omega_{\mathrm{B}}\cos\varphi,ζ(ΩB​,φ)≃ζ(0)+χZZ​ΩB​cosφ, (17)

where ζ(0)\zeta(0)ζ(0) is the value without the second tone and χZZ\chi_{ZZ}χZZ​ is derived in Appendix A.3. The phase selects the sign of the change and the amplitude sets its size. Choosing them so that ζ=0\zeta=0ζ=0 removes the ZZZZZZ term and yields the ideal bSWAP Hamiltonian in Eq. (9).

The same control can also be used to enhance the ZZZZZZ interaction. The resulting operation combines even-parity exchange with a conditional phase. It is the bSWAP counterpart of fSim gates, which instead exchange populations within the odd-parity subspace [28]. It is locally equivalent to an XXZXXZXXZ-type evolution and offers a route to Hamiltonian engineering [18]. The local equivalence, anisotropy, and isotropic Heisenberg condition are given in Appendix D.

III. Experimental demonstration

We use a superconducting processor designed at RIKEN and operated at The University of Osaka. The device comprises far-detuned, fixed-frequency transmons with fixed couplings arranged on a square lattice. The two qubits are labeled QA\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{A}}QA​ and QB\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{B}}QB​ as in Sec. II. Their parameters are listed in Table 1, with transition frequencies used for qubit control. Microwave pulses are generated by QuEL-1 SE hardware [29] and Qubex [30]. Calibrated DRAG pulses implement single-qubit gates [31]. The two qubits are read out simultaneously by dispersive measurement.

The strong exchange drive is applied to QA\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{A}}QA​, and a weak tone on QB\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{B}}QB​ at the same drive frequency cancels the accumulated ZZZZZZ phase. Figure 3 shows the two-tone control and the pulse envelopes. Quasi-adiabatic ramps with a counter-diabatic quadrature connect the undriven and dressed computational states [32, 33]. The benchmarked bSWAP and bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​ gates have total durations of 278278278 and 150 ns150\,\mathrm{ns}150ns, respectively, including two 161616-ns ramps. Both use a drive frequency of 4.324 GHz4.324\,\mathrm{GHz}4.324GHz and an estimated flat-top drive amplitude of ΩA/2π≃419 MHz\Omega_{\mathrm{A}}/2\pi\simeq 419\,\mathrm{MHz}ΩA​/2π≃419MHz, inferred from the measured ac Stark shift (Appendix B). The ramp design and gate calibration procedures are described in Appendix C.

III.1. Resonant exchange under strong driving

The amplitude-dependent resonance predicted in Sec. II.2 is visible directly in spectroscopy. Figure 4 shows the responses of QA\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{A}}QA​ and QB\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{B}}QB​ to a fixed-duration drive on QA\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{A}}QA​. At weak drive, the common bSWAP resonance ridge lies near the midpoint between the undriven qubit frequencies and shifts to lower frequency as the drive amplitude increases. The marked gate setting at 4.324 GHz4.324\,\mathrm{GHz}4.324GHz is about 81 MHz81\,\mathrm{MHz}81MHz below the midpoint. The orange curves, calculated from the device parameters, closely follow the measured resonance ridge. Independent Stark-Ramsey measurements calibrate the relation between ΩA\Omega_{\mathrm{A}}ΩA​ and the amplitude setting of the control electronics at several drive frequencies. We interpolate this relation across drive frequency to plot the model curves (Appendix B.2). The full frequency window and the simultaneously measured nearby-qubit responses are given in Appendix B.1.

The drive activates coherent exchange between ∣00⟩\lvert 00\rangle∣00⟩ and ∣11⟩\lvert 11\rangle∣11⟩. Figure 5 shows the QA\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{A}}QA​–QB\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{B}}QB​ populations versus drive frequency and pulse duration at a fixed amplitude setting. The population oscillations form a chevron pattern near 4.324 GHz4.324\,\mathrm{GHz}4.324GHz. In Fig. 5, readout-error mitigation is applied using calibrated confusion matrices.

The frequency–duration scan provides the initial operating point. We then refine the pulse duration by fitting data from repeated-pulse measurements. The local phases are removed by virtual-ZZZ updates [34]. The drive frame and qubit frames rotate at different frequencies. We compensate the phase shifts associated with the position of the gate in a circuit using the bSWAP pulse phase and virtual-ZZZ frame updates. Appendix C.2 describes the pulse-duration calibration and phase-correction procedures.

III.2. ZZ-free bSWAP gates

The ZZZZZZ phase accumulated during a bSWAP pulse of duration TTT is

ΦZZ=14∫0Tζ(t) dt,\Phi_{ZZ}=\frac{1}{4}\int_{0}^{T}\zeta(t)\,\mathrm{d}t,ΦZZ​=41​∫0T​ζ(t)dt, (18)

corresponding to UZZ=exp⁡(−iΦZZZZ)U_{ZZ}=\exp(-\mathrm{i}\Phi_{ZZ}ZZ{})UZZ​=exp(−iΦZZ​ZZ). To cancel this phase, we keep the bSWAP pulse on QA\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{A}}QA​ fixed and add a siZZle tone on QB\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{B}}QB​. We set its relative phase φ\varphiφ so that its contribution to the ZZZZZZ phase is opposite in sign to the accumulated phase, and then adjust the siZZle amplitude ΩB\Omega_{\mathrm{B}}ΩB​ to bring ΦZZ\Phi_{ZZ}ΦZZ​ to zero. In independent measurements, we confirmed that the residual ZZZZZZ phases were reduced to 1.4×10−3π1.4\times 10^{-3}\pi1.4×10−3π and 6.6×10−4π6.6\times 10^{-4}\pi6.6×10−4π for the bSWAP and bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​ gates, respectively (Appendix C.2).

Figure 7 shows that the accumulated ZZZZZZ phase can be tuned through zero by varying the relative phase or amplitude of the siZZle tone. The phase scans use a siZZle amplitude setting equal to 2%2\%2% of the bSWAP amplitude setting. In the amplitude scans, φ\varphiφ is held at its calibrated value for each gate.

With the ZZZZZZ phase compensated, we evaluate the Clifford bSWAP gate by interleaved randomized benchmarking (IRB) [35, 36]. For the non-Clifford bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​ gate, we instead use interleaved cross-entropy benchmarking (XEB) [37]. IRB gives a fidelity of 98.78%98.78\%98.78% for the 278278278-ns bSWAP gate, with a 95%95\%95% statistical interval of [98.61,98.96]%[98.61,98.96]\%[98.61,98.96]% [Fig. 7(a)]. XEB gives a fidelity of 99.34%99.34\%99.34% for the 150150150-ns bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​ gate, with a 95%95\%95% statistical interval of [99.27,99.42]%[99.27,99.42]\%[99.27,99.42]% [Fig. 7(b)]. The benchmarking protocols and an additional IRB measurement of a two-pulse bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​ block are described in Appendix E.

Figure 8 compares the excess errors relative to the coherence limit for bSWAP with and without ZZZZZZ compensation and for echoed CR. Using the T1T_{1}T1​ and T2,echoT_{2,\mathrm{echo}}T2,echo​ values in Table 1 with the coherence-limit expression in Ref. 38, we obtain reference fidelities of 99.42%99.42\%99.42% for the 278278278-ns bSWAP and 99.44%99.44\%99.44% for the 268268268-ns echoed CR gate. The ZZZZZZ-compensated bSWAP result is taken from Fig. 7(a). The excess errors are 0.910.910.91 and 0.640.640.64 percentage points for bSWAP without and with ZZZZZZ compensation, respectively, and 0.560.560.56 percentage points for CR.

We also demonstrate direct Bell-state preparation using a single 150150150-ns bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​ pulse, which prepares the even Bell state (∣00⟩+i∣11⟩)/2(\lvert 00\rangle+\mathrm{i}\lvert 11\rangle)/\sqrt{2}(∣00⟩+i∣11⟩)/2​ from ∣00⟩\lvert 00\rangle∣00⟩. After initial-state heralding, we reconstruct the density matrix by maximum-likelihood estimation using the readout confusion matrix. The Bell-state fidelity is 98.74%98.74\%98.74%, with a 95%95\%95% statistical interval of [98.02,99.38]%[98.02,99.38]\%[98.02,99.38]%. The preparation uses no siZZle tone because the ZZZZZZ interaction contributes only a global phase within the even-parity subspace.

IV. Discussion

IV.1. Complementary roles of bSWAP and CR

The benefit of a native interaction depends on the operation to be synthesized. CR supplies one Cartan axis, while bSWAP exchange supplies two equal axes. Their ideal interaction times therefore differ for CNOT and SWAP operations [39, 19]. The CNOT construction requires two bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​ gates, compared with one RZX(π2)R_{ZX}(\frac{\pi}{2})RZX​(2π​) gate for CR. The SWAP construction requires three native two-qubit gates in either case. These different gate counts lead to different conditions for a speed advantage (Appendix G.2).

The implementations of CNOT and SWAP on QA\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{A}}QA​–QB\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{B}}QB​ show this target dependence (Table 2). The CR- and bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​-based implementations are compared at matched drive amplitudes inferred from Stark shifts. CR gives a 26%26\%26% shorter CNOT with higher fidelity. The bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​-based SWAP is 33%33\%33% shorter and also has higher fidelity. Selecting the native gate for each target operation can therefore make circuit compilation more efficient. Comparison details are given in Appendix G.

Frequency collisions provide another motivation for complementary native interactions [5, 6]. The CR drive is tied to the target-qubit transition, whereas the Stark bSWAP drive frequency and amplitude can be chosen together along the resonance curve. This freedom may help avoid unwanted resonances, with a trade-off in exchange rate and required drive amplitude.

Native bSWAP gates may also serve as building blocks for quantum error correction. Dynamic surface-code circuits have been demonstrated using iSWAP gates in place of conventional CNOT/CZ gates [40]. Since bSWAP is locally equivalent to iSWAP, analogous circuits could be implemented using native bSWAP gates and local single-qubit rotations. Compensating the accompanying ZZZZZZ phase is important for realizing the intended Clifford operation in such circuits.

IV.2. Multilevel effects on gate speed

The analytical description of native Stark bSWAP in Ref. 19 is based on a two-level model. Our multilevel treatment includes drive-induced mixing with higher transmon levels. With the same hardware limit on drive amplitude, the two-level model does not permit a bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​-based construction with a shorter ideal CNOT interaction time than CR (Appendix G.2). Our multilevel model instead predicts this speed advantage at large qubit detuning and strong drive, where JXY>2JZXJ_{XY}>2J_{ZX}JXY​>2JZX​. The matrix elements determining the bSWAP and CR coefficients respond differently to this mixing, which changes the gate-speed comparison (Fig. 16).

Realizing this predicted regime requires control hardware capable of delivering stronger drives with high amplitude stability. Amplitude fluctuations shift the dressed-state splitting, detuning the two-photon resonance and changing the accumulated local phases.

IV.3. Applications to quantum simulation

Native access to the XX−YYXX-YYXX−YY interaction provides a direct route to quantum simulation of spin-squeezing dynamics. For the two-qubit collective spin Sμ=(σμA+σμB)/2S_{\mu}=(\sigma_{\mu}^{\mathrm{A}}+\sigma_{\mu}^{\mathrm{B}})/2Sμ​=(σμA​+σμB​)/2 with μ=x,y,z\mu=x,y,zμ=x,y,z, the Hamiltonian in Eq. (9) takes the two-axis countertwisting form [41],

HXY=−JXY2(Sx2−Sy2).H_{XY}=-\frac{J_{XY}}{2}(S_{x}^{2}-S_{y}^{2}).HXY​=−2JXY​​(Sx2​−Sy2​). (19)

Partial evolution from ∣00⟩\lvert 00\rangle∣00⟩ can reduce transverse spin fluctuations while retaining a nonzero mean longitudinal spin.

The two-qubit measurements in Fig. 9 illustrate this application. We identify the squeezed spin direction using the method of Ref. [42]. An independent measurement along this direction yields a Wineland parameter [43] of ξR2=0.684\xi_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}{}=0.684ξR2​=0.684, with a 95%95\%95% statistical interval of [0.644,0.729][0.644,0.729][0.644,0.729], below the coherent-state SQL of ξR2=1\xi_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}{}=1ξR2​=1. This result uses initial-state heralding without readout-error mitigation. Preparation conditions and the definition and measurement of ξR2\xi_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}ξR2​ are given in Appendix F.

Control of the accompanying ZZZZZZ interaction also provides access to anisotropic spin models. On a phase-aligned bipartite lattice, a sublattice basis change maps XX−YYXX-YYXX−YY plus ZZZZZZ to XXZXXZXXZ interactions (Appendix D).

For example, collective spin squeezing has been predicted in short-range XXZXXZXXZ lattices for suitable anisotropies and initial states [44, 45]. Coherent averaging with isotropic exchange provides another proposed route to collective countertwisting within a protected spin manifold [46].

Realizing these applications would require driving many qubit pairs simultaneously. Accessing a wider range of interaction anisotropies would require stronger siZZle tones and joint calibration of the siZZle and bSWAP drives.

V. Conclusion

We demonstrated ZZZZZZ-free Stark bSWAP gates in far-detuned, fixed-frequency transmons using a strong exchange drive and a weak tone to compensate the accompanying ZZZZZZ phase. The 278278278-ns bSWAP had a fidelity of 98.78%98.78\%98.78% from IRB, and the 150150150-ns bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​ had a fidelity of 99.34%99.34\%99.34% from interleaved XEB. A single bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​ pulse directly prepared a Bell state from the ground state. The XX−YYXX-YYXX−YY interaction also generated two-spin squeezing below the SQL.

The CNOT and SWAP comparisons demonstrated the complementary roles of CR and bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​. CR gave a shorter CNOT with higher fidelity, while the bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​-based SWAP was 33%33\%33% shorter and also had higher fidelity. Selecting the native gate for each target operation can therefore make circuit compilation more efficient. Control of XX−YYXX-YYXX−YY and ZZZZZZ interactions also offers a route to quantum simulation of interacting spin systems.

A.5. Full-cosine transmon model

At zero offset charge, the isolated transmon Hamiltonian is written as 4ECn^2−EJcos⁡φ^4E_{\mathrm{C}}\hat{n}^{2}-E_{\mathrm{J}}\cos\hat{\varphi}4EC​n^2−EJ​cosφ^​, where n^\hat{n}n^ counts Cooper pairs and φ^\hat{\varphi}φ^​ is the superconducting phase [26, 27]. Its eigenenergies Em\mathcal{E}_{m}Em​ and eigenstates ∣m⟩\lvert m\rangle∣m⟩ define the undriven basis. We choose EJE_{\mathrm{J}}EJ​ and ECE_{\mathrm{C}}EC​ to reproduce the specified transition frequency and anharmonicity.

For each transmon, the energies and transition coefficients used in Sec. II.2 are

Em\displaystyle E_{m}Em​ =Em−E0−mωd,\displaystyle=\mathcal{E}_{m}-\mathcal{E}_{0}-m\omega_{\mathrm{d}},=Em​−E0​−mωd​, (51)
λm+1\displaystyle\lambda_{m+1}λm+1​ =⟨m∣n^∣m+1⟩⟨0∣n^∣1⟩,m≥0.\displaystyle=\frac{\langle m\rvert\hat{n}\lvert m+1\rangle}{\langle 0\rvert\hat{n}\lvert 1\rangle},\quad m\geq 0.=⟨0∣n^∣1⟩⟨m∣n^∣m+1⟩​,m≥0.

Eigenstate phases are chosen to make λm\lambda_{m}λm​ real and positive, with λ1=1\lambda_{1}=1λ1​=1. These coefficients define aaa and bbb in Eq. (4), without assuming bosonic commutation relations. Retaining adjacent-level transitions in the rotating-wave approximation gives Eq. (5). Thus, ggg is the exchange matrix element between the undriven states ∣10⟩\lvert 10\rangle∣10⟩ and ∣01⟩\lvert 01\rangle∣01⟩, and ΩA\Omega_{\mathrm{A}}ΩA​ retains its resonant two-level Rabi-frequency normalization.

Appendix B: Device characterization

B.1. Drive spectroscopy

Figure 10 extends the frequency–amplitude scan in Fig. 4 to the surrounding qubits. A flat-top probe pulse is applied to QA\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{A}}QA​ for a total of 500 ns500\,\mathrm{ns}500ns, including two 303030-ns ramps. The color scale shows the magnitude of the background-subtracted mean IQ response, normalized at each drive amplitude, rather than population.

In Fig. 10(b), the resonance line observed in both the QA\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{A}}QA​ and QB\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{B}}QB​ responses corresponds to bSWAP exchange between ∣00⟩\lvert 00\rangle∣00⟩ and ∣11⟩\lvert 11\rangle∣11⟩. The fringes near ωA/2π≃4.15 GHz\omega_{\mathrm{A}}/2\pi\simeq 4.15\,\mathrm{GHz}ωA​/2π≃4.15GHz are the direct one-photon response of QA\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{A}}QA​. A CR response is also visible in Q58\mathrm{Q}_{58}Q58​ near its transition frequency of 4.56 GHz4.56\,\mathrm{GHz}4.56GHz.

B.2. Drive-amplitude calibration

To calibrate the amplitude setting of the control electronics, we apply the off-resonant drive during the Ramsey waiting interval. Comparing the Ramsey oscillation frequencies with and without the drive gives the Stark shift, from which we infer the physical drive amplitude ΩA\Omega_{\mathrm{A}}ΩA​ using the model in Appendix A.5.

Writing the normalized amplitude setting as s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1]s∈[0,1], we define the frequency-dependent drive-amplitude scale Ω0(ωd)\Omega_{0}(\omega_{\mathrm{d}})Ω0​(ωd​) by ΩA=s Ω0(ωd)\Omega_{\mathrm{A}}=s\,\Omega_{0}(\omega_{\mathrm{d}})ΩA​=sΩ0​(ωd​). Stark-Ramsey measurements from 4.2604.2604.260 to 4.430 GHz4.430\,\mathrm{GHz}4.430GHz give the calibration shown in Fig. 12. The two weak-drive settings give scales that differ by at most 0.77%0.77\%0.77%. At the tested higher drive amplitudes, the inferred scales are less than 1%1\%1% below this calibration. The interpolated calibration is used for the theoretical resonance curves in Fig. 4.

Independent Stark-shift measurements at the bSWAP and CR drive frequencies give ΩA/2π=418.71\Omega_{\mathrm{A}}/2\pi=418.71ΩA​/2π=418.71 and 419.08 MHz419.08\,\mathrm{MHz}419.08MHz, respectively, for the amplitude matching used in Table 2.

Appendix C: Pulse implementation

C.1. Quasi-adiabatic ramps

Rapid ramps to the bSWAP resonance can induce nonadiabatic transitions, whereas slow passage through intervening resonances can populate unwanted states. For rapid, near-adiabatic transfer between undriven and target dressed states, we use a pulse that combines a smoothed quasi-adiabatic ramp with a counter-diabatic quadrature [32, 33, 50].

For the two-level reference H0(t)=12[−δAZ+Ωx(t)X]H_{0}(t)=\tfrac{1}{2}[-\delta_{\mathrm{A}}Z+\Omega_{x}(t)X]H0​(t)=21​[−δA​Z+Ωx​(t)X], define θ(t)=arctan⁡[Ωx(t)/∣δA∣]\theta(t)=\arctan[\Omega_{x}(t)/|\delta_{\mathrm{A}}|]θ(t)=arctan[Ωx​(t)/∣δA​∣], where δA=ωA−ωd\delta_{\mathrm{A}}=\omega_{\mathrm{A}}-\omega_{\mathrm{d}}δA​=ωA​−ωd​. We design the rising ramp, 0≤t≤τ0\leq t\leq\tau0≤t≤τ, by prescribing a smooth adiabaticity profile,

ϵ(t)=∣θ˙(t)∣δA2+Ωx(t)2=ϵmax⁡sin⁡2 ⁣(πtτ).\epsilon(t)=\frac{|\dot{\theta}(t)|}{\sqrt{\delta_{\mathrm{A}}^{2}+\Omega_{x}(t)^{2}}}=\epsilon_{\max}\sin^{2}\!\left(\frac{\pi t}{\tau}\right).ϵ(t)=δA2​+Ωx​(t)2​∣θ˙(t)∣​=ϵmax​sin2(τπt​). (52)

This profile vanishes smoothly at both ramp boundaries. Integrating with Ωx(0)=0\Omega_{x}(0)=0Ωx​(0)=0 and Ωx(τ)=Ωˉx\Omega_{x}(\tau)=\bar{\Omega}_{x}Ωx​(τ)=Ωˉx​ gives

sin⁡θ(t)\displaystyle\sin\theta(t)sinθ(t) =sin⁡θˉ[u−sin⁡(2πu)2π],\displaystyle=\sin\bar{\theta}\left[u-\frac{\sin(2\pi u)}{2\pi}\right],=sinθˉ[u−2πsin(2πu)​],
θˉ\displaystyle\bar{\theta}θˉ =arctan⁡Ωˉx∣δA∣,u=tτ.\displaystyle=\arctan\frac{\bar{\Omega}_{x}}{|\delta_{\mathrm{A}}|},\quad u=\frac{t}{\tau}.=arctan∣δA​∣Ωˉx​​,u=τt​.

The boundary condition gives ϵmax⁡=2sin⁡θˉ/(∣δA∣τ)\epsilon_{\max}=2\sin\bar{\theta}/(|\delta_{\mathrm{A}}|\tau)ϵmax​=2sinθˉ/(∣δA​∣τ). The falling ramp is the time reverse.

The counter-diabatic quadrature contributes Ωy(t)Y/2\Omega_{y}(t)Y/2Ωy​(t)Y/2 to H0(t)H_{0}(t)H0​(t), with

Ωy(t)=−δAΩ˙x(t)δA2+Ωx(t)2.\Omega_{y}(t)=-\frac{\delta_{\mathrm{A}}\dot{\Omega}_{x}(t)}{\delta_{\mathrm{A}}^{2}+\Omega_{x}(t)^{2}}.Ωy​(t)=−δA2​+Ωx​(t)2δA​Ω˙x​(t)​. (54)

The counter-diabatic quadrature has opposite signs on the rising and falling ramps and vanishes on the plateau.

C.2. Gate calibration and phase tracking

At a fixed drive amplitude, frequency–duration chevron patterns provide the initial resonance frequency and pulse duration. In repeated-pulse scans, we apply identical exchange pulses in succession and sweep the duration of each pulse while keeping the drive frequency and amplitude fixed. A cosine fit to the resulting population oscillations refines the pulse duration.

To calibrate the phases, we apply each gate to ∣0+⟩\lvert 0+\rangle∣0+⟩, ∣1+⟩\lvert 1+\rangle∣1+⟩, ∣+0⟩\lvert+0\rangle∣+0⟩, and ∣+1⟩\lvert+1\rangle∣+1⟩, where ∣+⟩=(∣0⟩+∣1⟩)/2\lvert+\rangle=(\lvert 0\rangle+\lvert 1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}∣+⟩=(∣0⟩+∣1⟩)/2​, and reconstruct the output states by two-qubit tomography. With the exchange angle fixed, a joint fit to the off-diagonal density-matrix elements determines the local phases and residual ZZZZZZ phase.

The independent residual-phase checks in Sec. III.2 average the estimates from coherence on the two qubits. Their 95%95\%95% statistical intervals, obtained from multinomial counting statistics, are [2.2,6.4]×10−3 rad[2.2,6.4]\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{rad}[2.2,6.4]×10−3rad for bSWAP and [−0.3,4.9]×10−3 rad[-0.3,4.9]\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{rad}[−0.3,4.9]×10−3rad for bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​.

Figure 12 uses the local-phase decomposition described in Ref. 19: two post-rotations for bSWAP and an additional pre-rotation for bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​. The pre-rotation in Fig. 12(b) is implemented through the bSWAP drive phase and virtual post-rotations, without physical ZZZ pulses. The required drive-phase adjustment is half the pre-ZZZ rotation angle because of the two-photon transition process.

Appendix D: Interaction anisotropy

The exchange and ZZZZZZ coefficients directly determine the interaction anisotropy. An XXX basis change on QA\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{A}}QA​ puts the interaction in the XXZXXZXXZ form,

Hint′\displaystyle H^{\prime}_{\mathrm{int}}Hint′​ =−14[JXY(XX+YY)+ζZZ],\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{4}\left[J_{XY}(XX+YY)+\zeta ZZ{}\right],=−41​[JXY​(XX+YY)+ζZZ], (55)
ΔXXZ\displaystyle\Delta_{XXZ}ΔXXZ​ =ζJXY.\displaystyle=\frac{\zeta}{J_{XY}}.=JXY​ζ​.

Here, ΔXXZ\Delta_{XXZ}ΔXXZ​ is the ratio of the coefficient of ZZZZZZ to that of XX+YYXX+YYXX+YY. In this transformed basis, ζ=0\zeta=0ζ=0 gives an XX+YYXX+YYXX+YY interaction, while ζ=JXY\zeta=J_{XY}ζ=JXY​ gives the isotropic Heisenberg interaction.

For a finite resonant pulse with local phases removed, we compare the integrated coefficients,

Δeff=∫0Tζ(t) dt∫0TJXY(t) dt.\Delta_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{\int_{0}^{T}\zeta(t)\,\mathrm{d}t}{\int_{0}^{T}J_{XY}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t}.Δeff​=∫0T​JXY​(t)dt∫0T​ζ(t)dt​. (56)

For the calibrated bSWAP and bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​ pulses, this gives Δeff=4ΦZZ/π\Delta_{\mathrm{eff}}=4\Phi_{ZZ}/\piΔeff​=4ΦZZ​/π and 8ΦZZ/π8\Phi_{ZZ}/\pi8ΦZZ​/π, respectively. The measured phases in Fig. 7 therefore correspond to sampled Δeff\Delta_{\mathrm{eff}}Δeff​ ranges of approximately −0.09-0.09−0.09 to 0.210.210.21 for bSWAP and −0.12-0.12−0.12 to 0.180.180.18 for bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​. Both include positive and negative anisotropy but remain below the isotropic point, Δeff=1\Delta_{\mathrm{eff}}=1Δeff​=1. Extending this range toward the isotropic point would require stronger siZZle tones and joint calibration of the siZZle and bSWAP drives.

Appendix E: Benchmarking protocols

E.1. Interleaved randomized benchmarking

We benchmark the native bSWAP using standard IRB [35, 51]. The reference and interleaved decay parameters, prefp_{\mathrm{ref}}pref​ and pintp_{\mathrm{int}}pint​, give the gate error under the depolarizing model,

rgate=34(1−pintpref).r_{\mathrm{gate}}=\frac{3}{4}\left(1-\frac{p_{\mathrm{int}}}{p_{\mathrm{ref}}}\right).rgate​=43​(1−pref​pint​​). (57)

The data in Fig. 7(a) are mean populations P(00)P(00)P(00) over 323232 random sequences at each depth, with one-standard-error bars. The reference and interleaved means are fitted separately to exponentials with free offsets.

The reference Cliffords use bSWAP and single-qubit gates, with one bSWAP as the interleaved operation.

For bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​, we instead benchmark a pair of pulses. Two consecutive 150150150-ns pulses with the same calibrated parameters form a 300300300-ns bSWAP block. This block is used in both the reference Clifford compilation and the interleaved operation (Fig. 14).

The block error is r2=1.54×10−2r_{2}=1.54\times 10^{-2}r2​=1.54×10−2. Assuming small additive errors for the two pulses [19], the per-pulse estimate is r1est=r2/2=7.70×10−3r_{1}^{\mathrm{est}}=r_{2}/2=7.70\times 10^{-3}r1est​=r2​/2=7.70×10−3. This gives an estimated fidelity of 99.23%99.23\%99.23%, with a 95%95\%95% statistical interval of [99.08,99.40]%[99.08,99.40]\%[99.08,99.40]%. This is a block-derived estimate rather than a direct single-pulse IRB measurement. The XEB and IRB-derived estimates are consistent within their reported statistical uncertainties, with overlapping 95%95\%95% intervals.

E.2. Interleaved XEB with single-qubit references

Interleaved XEB compares reference circuits containing random single-qubit layers [52, 53] with circuits that insert a 150150150-ns bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​ between the layers [37]. The reference omits two-qubit pulses without replacing them by idle periods. We evaluate both circuit sets using regression XEB scores [53]. The data in Fig. 7(b) use 646464 random circuits at each depth, with one-standard-error bars estimated by circuit bootstrap.

The reference XEB score combines the decay of each qubit with their product and therefore is not, in general, a single exponential [54]. We fit each qubit’s exponential decay separately to obtain λA\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}λA​ and λB\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}λB​. Their equivalent two-qubit depolarizing parameter is

pref=λA+λB+3λAλB5.p_{\mathrm{ref}}=\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}+3\lambda_{\mathrm{A}}\lambda_{\mathrm{B}}}{5}.pref​=5λA​+λB​+3λA​λB​​. (58)

The interleaved score gives pintp_{\mathrm{int}}pint​ from an exponential fit with a free offset. If the reference and interleaved parameters admit the same two-qubit depolarizing description, Eq. (57) gives the gate error [37]. The ZZZZZZ-compensated data in Fig. 7(b) give F=1−rgate=99.34%\mathcal{F}=1-r_{\mathrm{gate}}=99.34\%F=1−rgate​=99.34%, with a 95%95\%95% interval [99.27,99.42]%[99.27,99.42]\%[99.27,99.42]%.

Appendix F: Spin-squeezing measurements

Starting from ∣00⟩\lvert 00\rangle∣00⟩, we prepare the state in Fig. 9 using a 989898-ns pulse at 4.312 GHz4.312\,\mathrm{GHz}4.312GHz, including two 242424-ns ramps. Population oscillations indicate a rotation angle of approximately π/4\pi/4π/4 in the even-parity subspace.

We quantify squeezing using the Wineland parameter [43]

ξR2(ϕ)=2Var⁡(Sϕ)⟨Sz⟩2,\xi_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}{}(\phi)=\frac{2\operatorname{Var}(S_{\phi})}{\langle S_{z}\rangle^{2}},ξR2​(ϕ)=⟨Sz​⟩22Var(Sϕ​)​, (59)

where Sϕ=Sxcos⁡ϕ+Sysin⁡ϕS_{\phi}=S_{x}\cos\phi+S_{y}\sin\phiSϕ​=Sx​cosϕ+Sy​sinϕ is the transverse spin component at angle ϕ\phiϕ. Values below the coherent-state SQL of ξR2=1\xi_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}{}=1ξR2​=1 indicate spin squeezing. We measure the transverse spin fluctuations by applying collective rotations before population readout [42].

We scan the preparation-pulse duration at fixed drive frequency, amplitude, and ramp duration. At each duration, a sinusoidal fit to measurements at 161616 analysis angles identifies the squeezed axis. Independent measurements of the transverse variance along this axis and the mean longitudinal spin then determine ξR2\xi_{\mathrm{R}}^{2}ξR2​. The 95%95\%95% statistical intervals are obtained by multinomial bootstrap of the measured outcome counts.

Figure 14 shows the duration scan and the independent validation at 98 ns98\,\mathrm{ns}98ns, near the observed minimum. Both datasets use initial-state heralding without readout-error mitigation. The zero-duration point was measured without the preparation pulse. The increase at longer durations can arise from residual transverse variance due to preparation and readout errors, amplified by the decreasing ⟨Sz⟩2\langle S_{z}\rangle^{2}⟨Sz​⟩2 in the denominator.

Appendix G: Gate synthesis and comparison with CR

G.1. Gate constructions and ideal times

The implementation time depends on both the interaction coefficients and the rotations needed for the target operation. The coefficients JXYJ_{XY}JXY​ and JZXJ_{ZX}JZX​ in Eqs. (10) and (20) give the interactions

HbSWAP\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{bSWAP}{}}HbSWAP​ =−JXY4(XX−YY),\displaystyle=-\frac{J_{XY}}{4}(XX-YY),=−4JXY​​(XX−YY), (60)
HCR\displaystyle H_{\mathrm{CR}}HCR​ =JZX2ZX.\displaystyle=\frac{J_{ZX}}{2}ZX.=2JZX​​ZX.

With this normalization, bSWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}bSWAP​ and RZX(π2)R_{ZX}(\frac{\pi}{2})RZX​(2π​) each generate a maximally entangled state from a suitable product state in time π2J\frac{\pi}{2J}2Jπ​ when JXY=JZX=JJ_{XY}=J_{ZX}=JJXY​=JZX​=J. The coefficients therefore measure entanglement-generation rates on the same scale.

The Cartan decomposition describes a two-qubit gate by rotations along XXXXXX, YYYYYY, and ZZZZZZ [20]. CNOT and CZ belong to the same local-equivalence class and require one axis, whereas SWAP requires all three.

An XXX on QB\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{B}}QB​ reverses the YYYYYY component of UbSWAPU_{\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}}UbSWAP​​ while preserving XXXXXX. Two native pulses with these echoes therefore give RXX(−π2)R_{XX}(-\frac{\pi}{2})RXX​(−2π​) [Fig. 15(a)]. The echo also reverses ZZZZZZ, canceling an identical residual conditional phase from the two pulses.

An HHH on QA\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{A}}QA​ maps XXXXXX to ZXZXZX. The local rotations in panel (b) then give CNOT [20]. CR realizes the same local-equivalence class with one RZX(π2)R_{ZX}(\frac{\pi}{2})RZX​(2π​) and local rotations.

The SWAP construction uses both axes of each native pulse. Local basis changes transform XX−YYXX-YYXX−YY into XX+YYXX+YYXX+YY, XX+ZZXX+ZZ{}XX+ZZ, and YY+ZZYY+ZZ{}YY+ZZ, giving the three factors in Fig. 15(c). Since these Pauli products commute,

eiπ(YY+ZZ)/8eiπ(XX+ZZ)/8eiπ(XX+YY)/8\displaystyle e^{\mathrm{i}\pi(YY+ZZ{})/8}e^{\mathrm{i}\pi(XX+ZZ{})/8}e^{\mathrm{i}\pi(XX+YY)/8}eiπ(YY+ZZ)/8eiπ(XX+ZZ)/8eiπ(XX+YY)/8 (61)
=eiπ(XX+YY+ZZ)/4=eiπ/4USWAP.\displaystyle=e^{\mathrm{i}\pi(XX+YY+ZZ{})/4}=e^{\mathrm{i}\pi/4}U_{\mathrm{SWAP}{}}.=eiπ(XX+YY+ZZ)/4=eiπ/4USWAP​.

The CR route uses three CNOT operations, alternating their control directions. These constructions attain the minimum interaction times with instantaneous local operations [39]. Table 3 gives the times for constant interaction coefficients.
